name: arch-ports-aarch64
excerpts:
18|Package repositories

27|⚠️ Warning
28|There is no official Port for this architecture. A Port is made official via an approved RFC, and there is no RFC for this architecture. Any packages available for this architecture are:
29|not built with Arch Linux infrastructure,
30|not signed by Arch Linux staff, and
31|not hosted on Arch Linux domains/mirrors.
32|Packages may also be outdated, broken, or missing entirely.
33|Support is primarily provided by other Arch Linux users (i.e. not staff).
34|The community does maintain unofficial packages to facilitate research, development, and testing in preparation for an RFC. Coverage of [core] and [extra] packages is very good. Most official Arch Linux packages build and run without patches on this architecture.
35|There is no central GitLab namespace for aarch64-related forks of official package source repositories. But if a package does need modifications that cannot be merged, or have not yet been merged, into the official package, they are typically discoverable by examining an official package’s forks in GitLab. Most of the relevant forks can be found in the personal GitLab namespaces of solskogen and bschnei.
36|The AUR does not accept packages that do not have x86_64 in arch(), but adding aarch64 to arch() when it also contains x86_64 is permitted and encouraged.
38|Device support#
39|The linux package for this Port intends to support devices with mainline Linux support (i.e. those that do not require vendor-/device-specific patches). It also supports virtual hosts (e.g. Hetzner and AWS cloud compute resources).
40|Support for bare metal devices is entirely community-driven. The devices listed below are those reported by the community to be working with the kernel available in the package repositories:
41|ASUS Vivobook S15 S5507Q
66|Migrate from Arch Linux ARM#
67|For supported devices, it is possible to simply update pacman.conf to use one of the unofficial package repositories, however it is not without some degree of risk, and reverting is not possible. After changing pacman.conf, it is critical to reinstall all packages to avoid a broken system. As a result, it is important to confirm that all of the packages you need are available in the repository to which you intend to migrate.
68|Package repositories#
69|⚠️ Similar to the unofficial user repositories available for x86_64, the following repositories are community-maintained, and the same warning applies.
70|arch.bens.haus (ARMv8+)#
71|These repos are for ARMv8 (or v8.1) devices (e.g. Raspberry Pi 4). If your device supports ARMv8.2 (or later) instructions, these packages will work, but packages in drzee.net repos provide better support/performance.
72|These repositories primarily exist to support research into the cost/feasibility of ARMv8 support.
73|drzee.net (ARMv8.2+)#
74|These repos provide broad coverage of official Arch Linux packages and are well maintained. A status dashboard is available here. The build system runs on ARMv8.2 cloud infrastructure (i.e. no cross-compilation). The build host runs the unofficial packages that it itself builds.
75|⚠️ Packages are built for devices supporting the ARMv8.2 (and later) instruction sets only.
76|That means they will not work on the Raspberry Pi 4 or devices with the ARM Cortex-A53 or earlier CPUs.
77|There are 3 repos: core, extra, and forge.
82|[core]
83|Server = https://arch-linux-repo.drzee.net/arch/$repo/os/$arch
84|[extra]
85|Server = https://arch-linux-repo.drzee.net/arch/$repo/os/$arch
86|[forge]
87|Server = https://arch-linux-repo.drzee.net/arch/$repo/os/$arch
88|The repositories are hosted on AWS S3, which does not generate directory listing/indexes for directory trees.
89|To access the directory listing/index for a given repository, add a ‘/’ at the end of the repository path, e.g. https://arch-linux-repo.drzee.net/arch/core/os/aarch64/.
90|Only the leaf folder can be browsed; other parts of the tree are not browsable (e.g. https://arch-linux-repo.drzee.net/arch/), and an “access denied” message will be shown.
91|The package signing key is available here: https://arch-linux-repo.drzee.net/arch/extra/os/aarch64/public.key
92|Bootstrap tarballs built with the packages in these repos are available here: https://arch-linux-repo.drzee.net/arch/tarballs/os/aarch64/
93|Installation and recovery ISO images for supported devices are available here:
94|https://codeberg.org/ironrobin/archiso-aarch64/releases/latest
95|Cloud images#
96|Amazon Web Services - EC2#
97|A cloud image for use with AWS is built approximately every 15 days. The current AMI ID can be found here and is only available in the eu-central-1 region.
98|To run on AWS you will need to set up an AWS account and spin up an EC2 instance using the AMI.
99|Setup AWS account, make sure to follow all steps including securing the account with an MFA token!
102|Get involved#
103|If you are comfortable running the unofficial packages provided by the community on your ARM device, please join us! We are having a lot of fun getting Arch running on our Raspberry Pis and ARM laptops.
104|If you have a device with mainline Linux support, but it is not in the list of devices confirmed to be working, consider testing and contributing to kernel configuration as needed to bring support to your device.
105|If you are having issues with a specific package, please determine whether it is aarch64-specific or not before raising. Do not open aarch64-specific Work Items on upstream packages. Instead, consider: fixing the issue and submitting a merge request, creating a Work Item on one of the user-maintained forks, or reaching out on IRC.
106|One of the primary pre-RFC efforts is identifying packages that require relatively straightforward changes to build on non-x86_64 architectures and submitting those changes to the official package for consideration. See here for an example.
107|Generic aarch64-related Work Items (issues unrelated to specific packages) are tracked here.
108|CPU features#
109|ARMv8-A is the first version of the ARM architecture to support 64-bit instructions. Since its introduction in 2011, there have been many extensions (ARMv8.2-A, etc.) of the original instruction set. In many cases, these extensions add new CPU instructions or require manufacturers to implement features that were only optional in prior versions.
110|For example, the Raspberry Pi 4 uses the Cortex-A72, which implements the ARMv8-A instruction set, while the Raspberry Pi 5 uses the Cortex-A76, which implements ARMv8.2-A extensions. This table is a helpful reference for understanding which products and CPUs use which version.
111|Be aware that a CPU generally advertised as being a certain version may have different features depending on its purpose in the final product. lscpu can provide helpful information for determining exactly what features/flags are supported by a specific CPU. Sample output for a Cortex-A53 (ARMv8-A):

132|Architecture: aarch64
133|CPU op-mode(s): 32-bit, 64-bit

name: alarm-signing
excerpts:
95|Package Signing
96|Arch Linux ARM implements package signing following the model created by Arch Linux. All packages in all repositories for all architectures are signed by our build system; however, the repository database files are not signed in order to limit the exposure of private keys and because it is technically unnecessary.
97|Since all of the packages in our repositories originate from our build system — not from individual developers and maintainers — the packages are signed by the single build system key before leaving the secure build environment. Additionally, Arch Linux ARM mirrors are synchronized via rsync push from our master server, furthering the integrity of packages available for installation.
98|Enabling Signature Checking
99|To help pacman-key work, ensure the haveged daemon is running. This daemon keeps the system's entropy pool full.
104|systemctl enable haveged
105|Initialize the pacman keyring:
106|pacman-key --init
107|Install the Arch Linux ARM keyring:
108|pacman -S archlinuxarm-keyring
109|pacman-key --populate archlinuxarm
110|Edit /etc/pacman.conf and uncomment or add the following lines:
111|SigLevel = Required DatabaseOptional
112|LocalFileSigLevel = Optional

1|# Stubble
2|
3|A minimal UEFI kernel boot stub that serves a single purpose:
4|
5|**Loading machine specific device trees embedded within a
6|kernel image.**
7|
8|stubble is compatible with [systemd-stub(7)](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/plucky/man7/systemd-stub.7.html)
9|and [ukify(1)](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/plucky/man1/ukify.1.html).
10|It is designed to seamlessly integrate with Ubuntu's current bootloader and
11|boot security model. The resulting kernel image can be signed and verified
13|
14|Before loading the kernel, the stub generates
15|[hwids](https://github.com/fwupd/fwupd/blob/main/docs/hwids.md) of the
16|running machine derived from smbios and compares them to an embedded
17|lookup table in the .hwids section of the kernel image.
18|If a match is found it loads the corresponding device tree from the
19|.dtbauto section before jumping tothe bundled kernel.
20|
23|- `debug`: Enable debug logging
24|- `stubble.dtb_override=true/false`: Enable or disable device-tree compat based dtb lookup. The default is `true`.
25|
26|## Dependencies
33|

35|
36|```
41|
42|Stubble supports three mechanisms for selecting a device-tree, tried in the
43|following order:
44|
45|### 1. HWID-based matching (no firmware device-tree needed)
46|
47|If no device-tree has been installed by the firmware, hardware ID values (HWIDs)
48|in the SMBIOS table are used to select one of the appended device-trees. This
49|mechanism is used for boards that only come with ACPI tables where the kernel
50|does not support booting via ACPI.
51|
52|The HWID based rules must be supplied as a directory with JSON files using the
53|`--hwids` parameter to ukify. The `.txt` files in hwids/txt are generated with
54|`hwids.py` and converted to `.json` files by running `hwid2json.py` from the
55|`hwids` directory. The `compatible` field of the resulting JSON files has to be
56|filled in manually.
57|
60|If a device-tree has been installed by the firmware as an EFI configuration
61|table, Stubble compares the `compatible` string of that device-tree to the
62|`compatible` strings of the appended device-trees. If a match is found, the
63|pre-installed device-tree is replaced by the one coming with Stubble.
64|
65|### 3. Model-based matching via machdb (pre-installed firmware device-tree needed)
66|
67|If compatible string matching fails and a `.machdb` section is present, Stubble
68|extracts the `model` property from the firmware-provided device-tree and looks
69|it up in the machdb database. The machdb maps model strings to device-tree
88|
89|Use parameter --machdb <file> for stubblify.
90|
91|### 4. Fallback to pre-installed device-tree
97|
98|Systemd's ukify tool can be used to append a kernel, device-trees in flattened
99|device tree format (DTB), hardware ID JSON files, and optionally a machdb file
100|to the Stubble stub.
101|
102|For a simple combined kernel+stubble image bundling a single DTB you can run:
103|
104|```
105|$ stubblify build --linux=/boot/vmlinuz --stub=stubble.efi --hwids=hwids/json \
106|--devicetree-auto=/boot/dtb --output=vmlinuz.efi
107|```
113|```
114|$ stubblify build --linux=/boot/vmlinuz --stub=stubble.efi --hwids=hwids/json \
115|--devicetree-auto=/boot/dtb1 --devicetree-auto=/boot/dtb2 \
116|--machdb=machdb.txt --output=vmlinuz.efi
123|If you would like to add support for a device that please open a pull request
124|adding the output of `sudo fwupdtool hwids` as a new file in `hwids/txt`.
125|
126|# Acknowledgements
128|This project is originally based on
129|[systemd-stub](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/plucky/man7/systemd-stub.7.html)
130|from the systemd project.
131|The `.dtbauto` feature in systemd was contributed by
134|project by Nikita Travkin and
135|[DtbLoader.efi](https://github.com/aarch64-laptops/edk2/tree/dtbloader-app)
136|from the aarch64-laptops project.
